summary: A short but real uphill forest hike to Wat Pha Lat: roots, shaded paths and a contemplative temple stop rather than a big summit expedition. Shortlist it if you want gentle adventure close to Chiang Mai and enjoy earning your temple visit on foot. Allow extra time for the return and transport; continuing to Doi Suthep substantially changes the difficulty.
whyGo: Combine a forest walk with an atmospheric working temple and mountain scenery.
Fits a morning without committing to a remote full-day trek.
bestFor: Moderately fit walkers comfortable on uneven ground
Temple lovers, photographers and travellers seeking a quieter morning
skipIf: You need step-free access or have difficulty descending roots and rocks.
You want a strenuous wilderness trek or guaranteed solitude.
duration: Plan 2–3 hours including the temple and local transfers. Olsen Tours estimates 45 minutes uphill and 30 minutes down, before sightseeing.
cost: Budget THB 100 per foreign adult for trail entry, plus transport and optional donations. A current local operator explicitly excludes this fee from its tour. Confirm at the checkpoint; no official tariff was located.
hours: A definitive official trail/checkpoint timetable was not verified. Walk in daylight, start early, and confirm access locally rather than relying on unrestricted map access.
bestTime: Early morning for cooler walking and a less busy temple; avoid setting out late or during heavy rain.
gettingThere: Take a taxi or songthaew to the mapped Monk’s Trail trailhead west of Chiang Mai University, near the end of Pilgrim’s Path. Download the pin beforehand. Agree a return pickup or retrace the trail; do not assume a taxi will wait at the temple.
booking: An independent walk generally needs no tour booking; verify current checkpoint requirements. A guide and driver can simplify navigation or a one-way walk. Obtain an exact quote directly from an operator.
accessibility: Uneven uphill trail, roots and slippery surfaces make this unsuitable for wheelchairs and many limited-mobility visitors. Road access to Wat Pha Lat is an alternative, but temple pathways also require care.
practicalTips: Wear shoes with grip and carry water, insect repellent and an offline map.
Cover shoulders and legs for the temple, remove shoes where requested, and keep voices low.
Treat the much longer, steeper onward trail to Doi Suthep as a separate planned outing.
decemberNotes: December is a sensible cool-season candidate, especially early in the day. This is a seasonal planning judgement, not a forecast: check rain, air quality and park notices shortly before walking. Holiday visitors can make the temple busier; shaded ground can remain slippery.
uncertainties: Official current trail hours, closures and fee exemptions were not independently confirmed.
Transport fares and guide prices vary; no reliable fixed return fare was verified.
